questions.question: When should you choose GraphQL over REST, and vice versa?
questions.title: GraphQL vs REST — When to Choose Each
questions.direct_answer: Choose **GraphQL** when clients need flexible data fetching, you have multiple client types with different data needs, or you want to reduce over-fetching and under-fetching. Choose **REST** when you need simplicity, caching via HTTP, file uploads, or when your API consumers expect standard HTTP conventions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can match a real workload (mobile vs web, narrow reads vs nested graphs, public API vs internal) to GraphQL or REST, and explain the operational cost of each — caching, rate-limiting, schema governance.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Picking GraphQL because it is newer, then discovering that CDN caching, per-field authorization, and rate-limiting all get harder and over-fetch just moves server-side. Or picking REST for a highly nested mobile UI and shipping 6 round-trips where one GraphQL query would suffice.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss query complexity analysis and cost-based rate limiting, persisted queries for cache-friendliness, GraphQL federation vs BFFs, and cases where hybrid (REST for writes + GraphQL for reads) outperforms either alone.

sections.title: The Real Trade-off: Who Decides What Data Comes Back?
sections.content:
The choice between GraphQL and REST isn't about which technology is "better" — it's about **who controls the shape of the response**.
- In REST, the server owns the data contract. `GET /api/users/123` returns the same 47 fields whether you're a mobile app that needs three or a dashboard that needs all of them.
- When your product has a single web frontend, that's fine — you design endpoints around the UI and move on.

The pain starts when clients multiply.
- A mobile app needs compact payloads over cellular networks.
- A partner integration needs five fields.
- An internal dashboard needs everything plus computed aggregates.
- REST's answer is either **over-fetching** (send everything, let clients ignore what they don't need), **under-fetching** (clients make multiple round trips to compose the data they need), or custom endpoints per client (`/api/users/summary`, `/api/users/full`).
- All three create maintenance burden that scales with client count.

GraphQL addresses this by making the client describe the data shape.
- A single `/graphql` endpoint accepts a query document specifying exactly which fields are needed, including nested relationships.
- The server resolves exactly that — nothing more.
- But this shift introduces its own costs: HTTP caching requires extra infrastructure since most GraphQL requests use `POST`, observability gets harder because every request hits the same URL, and the learning curve for schema design, resolver architecture, and `DataLoader` batching is real.
- The question is never "GraphQL or REST" in the abstract — it's whether your specific client diversity and data-fetching pain justify that operational investment.

sections.title: Where Each Approach Actually Wins and Loses
sections.content:
| Dimension | GraphQL | REST |
|---|---|---|
| Data shape | Client defines — request only what you need | Server defines — fixed response per endpoint |
| Over-fetching | Eliminated by design | Common — mobile gets desktop-sized payloads |
| Under-fetching (N+1 HTTP calls) | Solved — traverse relationships in one query | Requires careful endpoint design or BFF |
| HTTP caching | Requires persisted queries or APQ for CDN/browser caching | Native — `GET` + `Cache-Control` works with every CDN |
| File uploads | Multipart spec exists but is non-standard | Straightforward multipart/form-data |
| Schema evolution | Add fields freely, `@deprecated` old ones — no /v2 needed | Typically /v1, /v2 or content negotiation |
| Tooling breadth | Growing (GraphiQL, Apollo Studio) but narrower | Vast — Swagger, Postman, OpenAPI codegen |
| Observability | Every request hits one URL — need query-level metrics | Path-based — access logs show resource popularity |
| Real-time | Subscriptions built-in (WebSocket/SSE) | Requires separate WebSocket/SSE infrastructure |
| Learning curve | Schema design, resolvers, DataLoader, cost analysis | Well-understood by virtually every backend dev |

sections.title: Concrete Signals for Choosing One Over the Other
sections.content:
**Choose REST when** you have a single frontend with well-understood data requirements, when HTTP caching at the CDN and browser level is critical for performance, when your API is public-facing and consumers expect standard HTTP conventions, or when your team has no GraphQL experience and needs to ship quickly. REST's advantages compound in these scenarios — browsers, CDNs, and reverse proxies understand `GET` + `Cache-Control` natively, and tools like OpenAPI generate client SDKs with zero effort.

**Choose GraphQL when** you serve multiple clients with divergent data needs (web, mobile, partner APIs), when you're building a Backend-for-Frontend that aggregates data from several microservices, or when your frontend teams are bottlenecked waiting for backend teams to create new endpoints for every UI change. The "client describes what it needs" model means frontend developers iterate on data requirements without backend deploys — a workflow acceleration that's hard to appreciate until you've experienced it.

**The hybrid approach is common in practice.** Many teams run REST for their public API (where caching and HTTP conventions matter) and GraphQL internally (where flexibility matters). The BFF pattern formalizes this — a thin GraphQL layer sits in front of REST microservices, giving frontends flexibility while keeping backend services simple.

The anti-pattern to avoid: choosing GraphQL because it's "modern" for a simple CRUD API with one client. You'll spend more time on schema design, DataLoader wiring, and query cost analysis than you would maintaining a few REST endpoints. If your mobile and web apps ask for the same data in the same shape, the problem GraphQL solves doesn't exist yet.

sections.title: Same Data, Three Ways — REST Multi-Call vs GraphQL vs gRPC
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Client-shaped queries eliminate over-fetching** — one round trip fetches exactly the nested graph each consumer needs, cutting mobile payload sizes by.
- **`POST /graphql` breaks HTTP caching** — CDNs and proxies understand `GET` + `Cache-Control` natively.
- **Schema evolution replaces versioning** — add fields freely, deprecate with `@deprecated`.
- **Resolver fan-out creates N+1 by default** — independent field resolution means 100 books with authors fires 101 queries unless you wire `DataLoader`.
- **Single endpoint complicates observability** — every request hits `POST /graphql`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
GraphQL and REST are not simply alternatives — they solve different client-server coupling problems, and the right choice depends on who controls the data shape and how many distinct clients your API serves.

**REST — fixed shapes, universal compatibility:**
- The server defines fixed endpoints that return fixed shapes, which works well until you have a mobile app that needs three fields and a dashboard that needs forty from the same resource
- Unmatched operational simplicity: HTTP caching works natively through `GET` + `Cache-Control`, curl and Postman work without configuration, and every CDN and load balancer understands the model
- The default for external-facing APIs — partners and browsers can't install protobuf compilers or learn a custom query language; REST's universality is a real advantage

**GraphQL — client-shaped queries:**
- Lets clients specify exactly what they need in a query document; a single `/graphql` endpoint serves every consumer, eliminating endpoint proliferation for teams with diverse clients
- For teams with three or more clients with divergent data needs, or stitching data from multiple backend services, GraphQL pays for itself within a sprint
- The flexibility comes at operational cost: `POST /graphql` breaks HTTP caching natively, so you need persisted queries for edge caching; observability requires field-level instrumentation since every request hits the same URL

**The critical trade-offs:**
- Schema design mistakes are expensive — a field name you publish is a public contract that's harder to evolve than a REST endpoint; breaking schema changes require migration strategies
- The N+1 problem emerges immediately: each resolver runs independently with no knowledge of siblings, so 100 books with authors fires 101 queries unless you wire DataLoader batching from day one

I recommend REST for one frontend and simple CRUD, GraphQL when you have three or more clients with divergent needs or complex multi-source data. Most production systems run both — REST at the edge, GraphQL as an internal BFF.

sections.title: The Problem: Three Competing Libraries and Which One Won
sections.content:
Before Spring Boot 2.7, Java teams building GraphQL APIs faced a fragmented ecosystem.
- Netflix DGS, graphql-java-kickstart, and graphql-java-tools all worked, but none integrated with Spring's annotation model, testing slices, or security filters the way REST controllers do.
- You'd wire up a `RuntimeWiring` manually, register `DataFetcher` beans by hand, and test by constructing `ExecutionInput` objects — all glue code that felt like a different framework entirely.

**Spring for GraphQL** (`spring-boot-starter-graphql`) solved this by making GraphQL a first-class citizen in Spring Boot.
- Schema files auto-discover from `src/main/resources/graphql/`.
- Resolvers use `@Controller` with `@QueryMapping` and `@MutationMapping` — the same annotation style as `@RestController`.
- Security integrates through the existing `SecurityFilterChain`.
- Testing uses `@GraphQlTest` slices with `GraphQlTester`.
- This isn't a third-party adapter — it's the official Spring project maintained by the core team.

The setup takes about ten minutes for a working endpoint. You need three pieces: a starter dependency, a `.graphqls` schema file, and an annotated controller. Everything else — the `GraphQL` engine instance, the HTTP endpoint at `/graphql`, the schema parsing — is auto-configured by Boot.

sections.title: Add the Starter — One Dependency Wires the Engine
sections.content:
The starter dependency pulls in graphql-java, the Spring GraphQL integration, and the auto-configuration that registers the engine, the HTTP handler, and schema discovery. You also need a web layer — either `spring-boot-starter-web` (MVC) or `spring-boot-starter-webflux` (reactive). The choice between MVC and WebFlux is independent of GraphQL; pick whatever your existing project uses.

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-graphql</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

With just these two dependencies and zero configuration, Boot registers a `POST /graphql` endpoint. The auto-configuration creates the `GraphQlSource`, loads schema files, and wires up exception handling. If you're using WebFlux, the same auto-configuration works — Boot detects the reactive stack and registers a WebFlux handler instead of an MVC one.

sections.title: Define the Schema — Convention Over Configuration for File Discovery
Write the Controller — Annotations That Match Schema Fields
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`spring-boot-starter-graphql`** — official Boot starter auto-configures the GraphQL engine, `/graphql` endpoint, and schema discovery without manual.
- **`src/main/resources/graphql/*.graphqls`** — Boot auto-discovers and merges all `.graphqls` files in this directory.
- **`@QueryMapping` / `@MutationMapping` match by method name** — the resolver method name must match the schema field name by default.
- **`@SchemaMapping` for nested fields hides N+1** — `Book.author` gets its own resolver called once per parent.
- **Not DGS, not kickstart** — Spring for GraphQL integrates natively with `@GraphQlTest`, Boot security, and the actuator.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Setting up Spring for GraphQL is three pieces: dependency, schema files, and resolver beans. The official Spring project is simpler to integrate than older libraries and provides native testing support.

**Dependency and auto-configuration:**
- Add `spring-boot-starter-graphql` and a web starter to `pom.xml`; Boot auto-configures the GraphQL engine and a `/graphql` HTTP endpoint with zero additional wiring or factory beans
- Drop schema files into `src/main/resources/graphql/` with a `.graphqls` extension; Boot discovers and merges them automatically, so you can split schemas by domain — `book.graphqls`, `author.graphqls` — and they compose into one schema

**Resolver conventions:**
- Resolvers are plain `@Controller` beans: `@QueryMapping` handles reads, `@MutationMapping` handles writes, `@SchemaMapping` resolves nested fields like `Book.author`
- Method names match schema field names by convention, so there's almost no boilerplate; use `@SchemaMapping(typeName, field)` explicitly only when names diverge

**What to wire from day one:**
- Enable GraphiQL in dev profiles so the team can explore the schema before any client code exists — it's a built-in IDE for your API
- Wire DataLoader for any `@SchemaMapping` that resolves to a related entity immediately, not after the N+1 problem surfaces in production; retrofitting DataLoader into existing resolvers is significantly harder

**Why Spring for GraphQL over alternatives:**
- Integrates natively with `@GraphQlTest` slice tests, Spring Security filters, and Actuator; older libraries like DGS work but lack this cohesion with the Spring ecosystem

I recommend enabling GraphiQL in dev and setting up DataLoader for nested fields on the first day of development — both are much easier to start with than to add retroactively.

questions.question: What are the differences between Query, Mutation, and Subscription in GraphQL?
questions.title: Query, Mutation, Subscription — Core Operation Types
questions.direct_answer: **query** is for read-only data fetching, **mutation** is for write operations that change server state, and **subscription** establishes a long-lived connection for real-time event streams. All three are defined in the **GraphQL** schema and resolved on the server, but they differ in execution semantics and transport requirements.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the three operation types at an execution-model level — queries run in parallel on fields, mutations run sequentially, subscriptions hold an open transport (WebSocket/SSE) and emit events.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running writes from queries ("GET that mutates") because GraphQL lets you — bypassing CSRF, caching, and the audit trail that mutations give you. Or trying to implement subscriptions over plain HTTP without the graphql-transport-ws protocol.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss subscription transport choices (graphql-ws vs graphql-sse), mutation ordering guarantees, per-operation timeouts, and why persisted queries are usually applied only to queries, not mutations.

sections.title: Why Mutations Execute Serially — The Design Decision Most People Miss
sections.content:
Most developers learning GraphQL treat Query, Mutation, and Subscription as just labels — "Query is for reading, Mutation is for writing." That understanding is correct but shallow, and it misses the execution guarantees that matter in production.

**Queries execute fields in parallel.** When you send a document with three root query fields — `user`, `orders`, `recommendations` — the GraphQL engine can resolve them concurrently because queries are guaranteed side-effect-free. This is a contract: if your query resolver writes to a database, you've violated the spec, and the engine's parallel execution may produce race conditions.

**Mutations execute top-level fields serially.** If you batch `createOrder` and `chargePayment` in one mutation document, GraphQL processes them in the order you wrote them — `createOrder` completes before `chargePayment` starts.
- This serial guarantee exists because writes have side effects and ordering matters.
- It's the GraphQL equivalent of a database transaction's sequential execution, though without rollback semantics — if `chargePayment` fails, `createOrder` is not automatically reversed.

**Subscriptions break the request-response model entirely.** They don't return a single result — the client sends one subscribe document and the server pushes events over a persistent connection, typically WebSocket.
- In Spring Boot, a `@SubscriptionMapping` method returns a `Flux<T>` that the framework streams to the client.
- This means your infrastructure requirements split: HTTP for queries and mutations, WebSocket for subscriptions, each with its own auth flow and timeout configuration.

sections.title: Execution Semantics That Affect Production Architecture
sections.content:
| Aspect | Query | Mutation | Subscription |
|---|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Read data, no side effects | Write/modify server state | Real-time event stream |
| Top-level field execution | Parallel (may be concurrent) | Serial (strict document order) | N/A — single subscribe field |
| Transport | HTTP POST (or GET for persisted) | HTTP POST | WebSocket or SSE |
| Response model | Single JSON response | Single JSON response | Multiple pushed payloads over time |
| Idempotency | Inherent — reads are safe | Must be designed explicitly | N/A — server pushes events |
| Spring annotation | `@QueryMapping` | `@MutationMapping` | `@SubscriptionMapping` |
| Return type in Spring | Object / `List<T>` | Object | `Flux<T>` / `Publisher<T>` |
| Auth consideration | Standard HTTP auth | Standard HTTP auth | WebSocket handshake auth — different flow |

sections.title: The Transport Split That Changes Your Infrastructure
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Query fields resolve in parallel** — the engine treats them as side-effect-free and may execute concurrently.
- **Mutation fields execute serially in document order** — `createOrder` completes before `chargePayment` starts.
- **Subscriptions need persistent transport** — WebSocket or SSE; Spring's `@SubscriptionMapping` returns a `Flux<T>` fed by Reactor sinks or message.
- **Auth differs per transport** — HTTP auth flows don't transfer to WebSocket without explicit handshake handling.
- **Backpressure is a subscription concern** — unbounded Reactor sinks grow in memory if clients can't keep up.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
GraphQL's three operation types differ in execution semantics, not just intent — understanding the difference prevents subtle bugs and incorrect assumptions about ordering and consistency.

**Queries — parallel, side-effect free:**
- Query fields resolve in parallel because the engine guarantees they are side-effect-free; it may safely run `user`, `orders`, and `recommendations` concurrently
- Writing to a database inside a query resolver violates this contract and risks race conditions — the engine may call it from multiple threads simultaneously

**Mutations — serial, with manual rollback:**
- Mutation top-level fields execute serially in document order by design — if you batch `createOrder` and `chargePayment` in one mutation document, they run in written order
- Critically, there is no automatic rollback — if `chargePayment` fails, the order is already created; compensating logic is your responsibility
- For complex multi-step mutations with rollback requirements, consider saga patterns or service-level transactions behind the resolver

**Subscriptions — persistent connection, different infrastructure:**
- Subscriptions break the request-response model: the client subscribes once and the server pushes events over WebSocket; in Spring Boot, return a `Flux` from `@SubscriptionMapping` fed by a Reactor sink
- The practical consequence most people miss is the transport split: queries and mutations are plain HTTP POST, so existing security filters and load balancers work; subscriptions need WebSocket infrastructure with its own auth flow, reconnection logic, and backpressure handling

I recommend keeping subscriptions on a separate concern from queries and mutations in your architecture — different transport, different auth model, different infrastructure requirements.

questions.question: How do DataFetcher and DataLoader work in graphql-java and Spring for GraphQL?
questions.title: How DataFetcher and DataLoader Work
questions.direct_answer: A DataFetcher is the low-level **resolver** interface in **GraphQL**-java — every field in the schema is backed by one. **DataLoader** is a batching and caching utility that groups multiple individual loads into a single bulk call, solving the **N+1** problem by deferring resolution until all fetchers in the current execution level have registered their keys.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Candidates who only know annotations but not the underlying DataFetcher mechanism will struggle with performance tuning.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Candidates who only know annotations but not the underlying DataFetcher mechanism will struggle with performance tuning.

sections.title: The Illusion of Annotation Magic — What Actually Runs Under @QueryMapping
sections.content:
When you annotate a method with `@QueryMapping` in Spring for GraphQL, the framework registers a `DataFetcher<T>` for you — but the annotation hides a critical performance reality.
- Every single field in your GraphQL schema is backed by a `DataFetcher`, and the engine calls each one independently during execution.
- For scalar fields on an object type, the default `PropertyDataFetcher` reads values via getter methods — you never see it, but it runs for every field on every object in the result.
- For computed or relational fields, you provide a custom fetcher through `@SchemaMapping`.

The independence is both the power and the trap.
- When the engine processes a list of 50 books and each book has an `author` field, it invokes the author `DataFetcher` 50 times — once per book, with zero coordination between calls.
- Each invocation hits the database independently: 50 singleton `SELECT * FROM author WHERE id = ?` queries plus the original books query makes 51 round trips.
- This is the N+1 problem, and it's not a bug — it's how field-level resolution is designed to work.

**DataLoader** is the coordination layer that fixes this.
- Instead of executing database calls immediately, each resolver calls `loader.load(key)` and receives a `CompletableFuture`.
- The engine collects all `load()` calls within one execution level, then dispatches them as a single batch — one `SELECT * FROM author WHERE id IN (1,2,...50)` replaces fifty singleton queries.
- Understanding how the engine walks execution levels and when DataLoader dispatches is the key to tuning GraphQL performance.

sections.title: How the Engine Walks the Schema — Level-by-Level Execution
sections.content:
The GraphQL execution engine processes your query as a tree, level by level. Consider the query `{ books { title author { name } } }`. The engine starts at the root `Query` type, calls the `books` DataFetcher, and gets back a list of 50 `Book` objects. That's **level 0**.

Now the engine descends to **level 1** — it needs to resolve `title` and `author` for each of the 50 books. For `title`, the default `PropertyDataFetcher` calls `book.getTitle()` — instant, no database call. For `author`, it invokes your custom DataFetcher 50 times. If that fetcher calls the repository directly, you get 50 queries. If it uses a DataLoader, each invocation registers a key and gets a `CompletableFuture` back.

After all DataFetchers at level 1 have been called (and all have registered their keys with the DataLoader), the engine triggers a **dispatch**. This is the moment DataLoader's batch function fires — it receives all 50 author IDs at once, executes one query, and completes all 50 futures with their results.

The engine then descends to **level 2** — resolving `name` for each `Author` object. Since `name` is a scalar with a `PropertyDataFetcher`, it's just a getter call. The tree walk is complete.

This level-by-level dispatch is why DataLoader works. If the engine resolved fields depth-first instead of breadth-first, there would be no batching window — each `load()` call would dispatch immediately.

sections.title: DataLoader's Batching Contract — What Your Batch Function Must Guarantee
Per-Request Cache and When It Works Against You
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Every field has a `DataFetcher`** — annotations like `@QueryMapping` register them behind the scenes.
- **Level-by-level execution creates the batching window** — the engine calls all DataFetchers at one depth before dispatching, which is why DataLoader can.
- **Batch result order must match input key order** — DataLoader maps by position, not by key lookup.
- **Per-request cache prevents duplicate loads** — two books with `authorId = 5` produce one database lookup.
- **Spring creates fresh registries per request** — `DataLoaderRegistry` is request-scoped automatically.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
DataFetcher is the resolver primitive in graphql-java — every single field in your schema has one, whether you wrote it explicitly or Spring registered it through `@QueryMapping`. For simple scalar fields like `title`, the default `PropertyDataFetcher` calls the getter. For relational fields like `Book.author`, you provide a custom fetcher.

**The N+1 performance trap:**
- The performance trap shows up on list queries: if you fetch fifty books and each book's `author` field fires its own database call, you get fifty-one total queries — one for books, fifty for authors
- Each resolver runs independently with no awareness of the other pending loads at the same level — this is by design, and DataLoader is the intended fix

**How DataLoader solves it:**
- Instead of hitting the database immediately, each resolver calls `authorLoader.load(id)` and gets back a `CompletableFuture`; the engine collects all load calls during one execution level, then dispatches them as a single batch — one `WHERE id IN (...)` replaces fifty singleton selects
- The engine's level-by-level execution creates the batching window: all DataFetchers at one depth complete before the next depth dispatches, which is why DataLoader can collect keys across siblings

**The non-negotiable ordering rule:**
- Your batch function must return results in the same order as the input key list — DataLoader matches results to parents by position, not by key lookup
- If you return them in database sort order instead, data silently attaches to the wrong parent objects — it looks like corruption but it's an ordering bug

**Per-request caching:**
- DataLoader caches within the request — two books sharing the same author ID produce one lookup; but if a mutation updates that author mid-request, call `loader.clear(id)` explicitly to prevent stale data

I recommend wiring DataLoader for every `@SchemaMapping` that resolves a related entity from the start — retrofitting is significantly harder after the N+1 problem is discovered in production.

questions.title: N+1 Problem in GraphQL and the BatchLoader Solution
questions.direct_answer: The **N+1** problem occurs when resolving a list of N items and each item triggers an additional database **query** for a nested field, resulting in N+1 total queries. The solution is **DataLoader**'s BatchLoader interface, which collects all requested keys within one execution level and issues a single batched database query.

sections.title: The Query Explosion You Don't See Until Production
sections.content:
The N+1 problem is the most common performance trap in GraphQL, and it's invisible in development. You test with five books in your local database and everything feels fast. In production, a client queries 200 books with authors — and suddenly your database connection pool is exhausted.

The math is simple but devastating. A query like `{ books { title author { name } } }` fetches the list of books with one SQL query. Then, for every book in the result, the `author` resolver fires a separate `SELECT * FROM author WHERE id = ?`. With 200 books, that's 201 database round trips. The response time isn't one query's latency — it's 201 queries' latency stacked sequentially, plus connection pool contention.

What makes this subtle is that it doesn't show up in unit tests (you mock the repository), it doesn't show up in integration tests with small datasets, and the resolver code looks completely correct — it returns the right data. The problem is structural: GraphQL's field-level resolution model treats each resolver as independent, with no automatic coordination between siblings.

sections.title: The Resolver That Looks Correct But Fires 201 Queries
Why Independent Field Resolution Creates This Pattern
sections.content:
The root cause is GraphQL's execution model. When the engine processes `Book.author` for a list of books, it invokes the `DataFetcher` once per book without any coordination. Each invocation has no knowledge of the other pending loads. This is fundamentally different from REST, where you would write a JOIN query or an `IN` clause upfront.

In REST, the endpoint handler controls the full query: `SELECT b.*, a.* FROM book b JOIN author a ON b.author_id = a.id`. One query, all data. In GraphQL, the books resolver and the author resolver are separate, independent functions. The books resolver doesn't know that authors will be needed, and the author resolver doesn't know how many siblings are pending.

This design is intentional — it enables composability. Any client can request any combination of fields without the server pre-planning joins for every possible query shape. But composability without coordination means the naive implementation fires one query per field per parent.

The detection signal is straightforward: enable SQL logging (`spring.jpa.show-sql=true` or a P6Spy profiler) and run a list query with a nested field. If you see repeated singleton selects with different parameter values, you have an N+1. In production, monitor the metric **queries per GraphQL request** — anything above 5-10 per request warrants investigation.

sections.title: The Fix — BatchLoader Collapses N Queries Into One
DataLoader Batching — How N+1 Becomes 1+1
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Without["Without DataLoader (N+1 queries)"]
        gql1["GraphQL\nResolver: Query.posts"] --> db1["DB: SELECT * FROM posts LIMIT 20\n(1 query)"]
        gql1 --> p1["Post 1 resolver: author"]
        gql1 --> p2["Post 2 resolver: author"]
        gql1 --> p3["Post 3 resolver: author"]
        gql1 --> pn["... Post N resolver: author"]
        p1 --> q1["DB: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=?"]
        p2 --> q2["DB: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=?"]
        p3 --> q3["DB: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=?"]
        pn --> qn["DB: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=?"]
    end

    subgraph With["With DataLoader (1+1 queries)"]
        gql2["GraphQL\nResolver: Query.posts"] --> db2["DB: SELECT * FROM posts LIMIT 20\n(1 query)"]
        gql2 --> r1["Post 1: authorLoader.load(id)"]
        gql2 --> r2["Post 2: authorLoader.load(id)"]
        gql2 --> r3["Post 3: authorLoader.load(id)"]
        gql2 --> rn["... Post N: authorLoader.load(id)"]
        r1 --> dl["DataLoader queue:\n[id1, id2, id3, ..., idN]"]
        r2 --> dl
        r3 --> dl
        rn --> dl
        dl --> batched["DB: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN (id1..idN)\n(1 batched query, results cached per-request)"]
    end
```

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **N+1 is invisible in dev** — tests pass, data is correct, but 200-row lists produce 201 queries.
- **Independent field execution is the root cause** — each `DataFetcher` runs in isolation with no knowledge of sibling resolvers.
- **`BatchLoader` collapses N loads into one `IN` query** — defers `load(key)` calls within an execution level, then dispatches a single batch.
- **`maxBatchSize` prevents unbounded IN clauses** — some databases struggle with 10K+ element lists.
- **Batching fixes count, not query quality** — if the foreign key column lacks an index, one `WHERE id IN (...)` over 200 keys still scans the full table.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The N+1 problem is the single most common performance trap in GraphQL. You fetch a list of two hundred books, and each book's `author` field fires its own database query independently. That's two hundred and one total round trips where two would suffice.

**Why it happens:**
- GraphQL resolves each field in isolation — the author resolver for book one has no idea that books two through two hundred are about to ask for authors; in REST you would write a JOIN upfront, but GraphQL's field-level execution model does not coordinate across siblings by default
- It's invisible in development because small datasets don't expose it — tests pass, data is correct, and the problem only appears when list sizes grow in production

**How DataLoader fixes it:**
- Each resolver calls `authorLoader.load(id)` and gets back a `CompletableFuture` instead of hitting the database immediately; the engine collects all those load calls during one execution level, then dispatches them as a single batch
- One `WHERE id IN (...)` replaces two hundred singleton selects — a transformation from O(n+1) database round trips to O(2)

**Critical implementation details:**
- Your batch function must return results in the same order as the input key list — DataLoader matches by position, not key lookup; returning results in database sort order silently attaches data to the wrong parent objects
- Set `maxBatchSize` to 100–250 to avoid enormous IN clauses that some databases struggle with; DataLoader automatically splits into multiple batches when the limit is reached
- Batching fixes call count, not query quality — a missing index on the foreign key column turns one large `IN` query into a full table scan; verify indexes before assuming the fix is complete

I recommend SQL logging in development and monitoring queries-per-request to detect N+1 issues before they reach production — they are invisible in small-data test scenarios.

sections.title: Why Schema Mistakes Are the Most Expensive Kind of Tech Debt
sections.content:
A REST endpoint can be quietly versioned or replaced — add `/v2/users`, deprecate `/v1/users`, migrate clients over time.
- A GraphQL schema change is visible to every consumer simultaneously.
- Removing a field breaks any client that queries it.
- Changing a non-null field to nullable changes the error-handling semantics.
- Renaming a type requires every query document to update.
- This makes schema design the highest-leverage decision in a GraphQL API — get it right and the schema evolves gracefully for years; get it wrong and you're stuck maintaining backward-compatible workarounds.

The most common mistake is **modeling the schema after your database**.
- Teams take their PostgreSQL table structure — snake_case column names, foreign key IDs, join table intermediaries — and expose it verbatim.
- Clients shouldn't know that `author_id` is a column in the `books` table.
- They should see `author: Author!` and traverse the relationship directly.
- The schema represents the **domain**, not the storage layer.

Three design decisions have the most production impact: **nullability** (which controls error propagation), **pagination shape** (which determines how lists evolve), and **mutation payloads** (which determine how clients handle errors). Getting these three right is more important than any individual field naming convention.

sections.title: Nullability Is an Error-Propagation Decision, Not a Type-Safety One
Relay Connections Give Lists Room to Evolve
Mutation Payloads and Errors-as-Data Keep Clients Sane
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Null bubbling is the schema's biggest production risk** — a non-null field failure cascades up the tree, potentially erasing an entire query response.
- **Relay Connections future-proof lists** — `edges/node/cursor/pageInfo` gives stable cursor pagination and room for edge metadata without breaking.
- **`UserError` in mutation payloads separates validation from system errors** — clients map `field: "title"` to form inputs instead of string-parsing the.
- **Enums enforce contracts at parse time** — `BookStatus` catches invalid values before your resolver runs.
- **Schema models the domain, not the database** — expose `author: Author!` not `authorId: String!`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Good GraphQL schema design starts with one rule: design for clients, not your database. Schemas where every database column shows up as a field, snake_case leaks from Postgres, and foreign key IDs are exposed instead of related objects are a common and expensive mistake.

**The nullability trap — the most critical production decision:**
- Overusing `!` non-null sounds like good type safety, but the real consequence is null bubbling — if a non-null field throws, GraphQL nulls the parent; if the parent is also non-null, it keeps cascading upward and can erase an entire query response from a single resolver failure
- Default nullable, mark only truly invariant fields like `id` as non-null, and tighten later as resolvers prove stable in production; loosening nullability later is a breaking change, tightening is non-breaking

**Pagination — Relay Connections from the start:**
- Use the Relay Connection pattern for all list fields: `edges`, `node`, `cursor`, and `pageInfo`; it feels like ceremony initially but gives stable cursor-based pagination and room for edge metadata without breaking clients when requirements evolve
- The alternative is returning a plain `[Book]!` list — which means breaking the schema when you later need pagination or edge-level data

**Mutation design:**
- Mutations should use dedicated input types and return payload types with a `UserError` list; validation failures come back as structured data that clients can map to form fields
- Reserve the top-level `errors` array for unexpected system failures — things the client can't recover from; use `UserError` for "title is required" or "email already taken"
- Enums and custom scalars like `DateTime` enforce contracts at parse time so invalid values fail at schema parsing, not in resolver code

I recommend establishing nullability conventions in your schema design guide before the first field is published — it's far easier to tighten nullability later than to deal with null bubbling in production.

sections.title: The Single-Endpoint Problem That Breaks URL-Based Security
sections.content:
In REST, authorization is often path-based — `/admin/**` requires `ROLE_ADMIN`, `/api/orders/**` requires authentication.
- Spring Security's `HttpSecurity.authorizeHttpRequests()` matches URL patterns, and you're done.
- This approach breaks completely with GraphQL because every operation — read, write, delete, admin, public — hits the same `/graphql` endpoint.

A URL-based rule like `.requestMatchers("/graphql").authenticated()` is useful as a baseline (block anonymous access entirely), but it can't distinguish between a public `books` query and an admin `deleteUser` mutation.
- Both are `POST /graphql` with a JSON body — only the query document differs.
- This means authorization in GraphQL must happen at a different layer: inside the resolvers, the service methods, or a custom GraphQL instrumentation.

Authentication is the easier part — it's identical to REST.
- A JWT filter validates the bearer token in the `Authorization` header, populates the `SecurityContext`, and the request continues.
- By the time the GraphQL engine processes the query, the authenticated principal is available through `SecurityContextHolder` or injected via `@AuthenticationPrincipal`.
- The complexity is entirely in authorization, and the right strategy depends on how granular your access control needs to be.

sections.title: Wire JWT Authentication — The Same Filter Chain as REST
Enforce Authorization at the Resolver Level — Where Granularity Lives
Map AccessDeniedException to GraphQL Errors — Not HTTP 403
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Single `/graphql` endpoint defeats URL-based authorization** — `requestMatchers("/graphql")` can't distinguish a public query from an admin mutation.
- **`@EnableMethodSecurity` is silently required** — without it, `@PreAuthorize` annotations are ignored and every operation runs with no role check.
- **`@AuthenticationPrincipal` injects identity without `SecurityContextHolder`** — keeps resolvers testable by accepting a mock `UserDetails` as a method.
- **`AccessDeniedException` must map to GraphQL `FORBIDDEN`** — without a `DataFetcherExceptionResolver`, auth failures become generic `INTERNAL_ERROR`.
- **Field-level auth belongs in the service layer** — checking field visibility in the resolver couples auth logic to the schema.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Authentication in a GraphQL Spring Boot API is identical to REST — a JWT filter validates the bearer token before the GraphQL engine sees the request, and the result goes into the `SecurityContext`. Authorization is where the GraphQL-specific concerns appear.

**Why URL-based auth rules don't work:**
- With REST you can write path-based rules like `/admin/**` requires `ROLE_ADMIN`, but with GraphQL every operation hits the same `/graphql` endpoint — URL rules cannot distinguish a public query from an admin mutation
- The solution is method-level security: `@PreAuthorize` on resolver methods — a query requires `isAuthenticated()`, a delete mutation requires `hasRole('ADMIN')`

**The silent failure — `@EnableMethodSecurity`:**
- Without `@EnableMethodSecurity`, `@PreAuthorize` annotations are silently ignored — everything appears to work, but no role checks actually run
- This passes code review because tests typically don't exercise authorization boundaries; always write a test that verifies an unauthenticated call is rejected

**Error mapping:**
- When `@PreAuthorize` rejects a call, Spring throws `AccessDeniedException`; GraphQL always returns HTTP 200, so without explicit handling this becomes a generic `INTERNAL_ERROR` that clients can't distinguish from a server bug
- Register a `DataFetcherExceptionResolver` that converts it into a typed FORBIDDEN error with an `extensions.code` field so clients can react programmatically

**Field-level authorization:**
- Inject `@AuthenticationPrincipal` to get the `UserDetails` directly in resolvers — keeps the resolver testable without `SecurityContextHolder`
- Field-level auth for sensitive fields like `salary` or `email` belongs in the service layer, not the resolver — it allows reuse across resolvers and prevents auth logic from being tightly coupled to the schema shape

I recommend writing authorization tests that verify specific `extensions.code` values on rejected operations — without them, auth failures are indistinguishable from server errors for both clients and your own monitoring.

questions.question: What are the differences between cursor-based and offset-based pagination in GraphQL?
questions.title: GraphQL Pagination — Cursor-Based vs Offset-Based
questions.direct_answer: **offset** **pagination** uses skip/limit parameters and is simple to implement but unstable when data changes during pagination. **cursor**-based pagination uses an opaque pointer to the last-seen item and is stable, scalable, and recommended for infinite scroll or real-time data. The Relay Connection spec formalizes cursor pagination and is the de facto standard for **GraphQL** APIs.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Exposing database offsets (or row IDs) as the "cursor" — clients reverse-engineer them and break when you add a sort. Or storing offset pagination in a URL that clients bookmark and share; it rots within hours.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why cursors should be opaque and encode the sort key + tie-breaker, how `ScrollSubrange` in Spring for GraphQL maps to JPA keyset pagination, and the subtleties of filter+sort stability with cursor-based pagination.

sections.title: The Pagination Bug That Only Appears When Data Changes
sections.content:
Pagination strategy seems like a minor implementation detail until users start reporting duplicate items in their feed. The root cause: offset-based pagination (`LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40`) assumes the dataset doesn't change between page fetches. When it does — a new order arrives, a post is deleted, a record moves in sort order — the window shifts.

Imagine a user scrolling through orders sorted by date.
- They fetch page 1 (items 1-20) and page 2 (items 21-40).
- Between fetches, a new order arrives and pushes everything down by one position.
- Page 3 (`OFFSET 40`) now starts at what was item 40 instead of item 41 — the user sees item 40 twice and never sees item 41.
- In a social feed with frequent updates, this happens on nearly every scroll.

**Cursor-based pagination** eliminates this by anchoring the position to a value in the data itself, not an offset number.
- Instead of "skip 40 rows," the query says "give me 20 rows after the row with `created_at = '2025-01-15T10:30:00' AND id = 847`." New inserts above or below don't shift the window — the cursor points to a stable position in the sorted index.
- The trade-off is losing random page access: you can't jump to "page 5" because there's no offset to calculate.
- For user-facing feeds and infinite scroll, that's an acceptable constraint.
- For admin grids where a support agent needs page 47, it's a dealbreaker.

sections.title: Where Each Strategy Breaks and Where It Shines
sections.content:
| Dimension | Cursor-Based | Offset-Based |
|---|---|---|
| Stability on inserts/deletes | Stable — cursor anchors to sort position | Unstable — window shifts, duplicates and gaps |
| SQL performance on deep pages | Constant — `WHERE (sort, id) > (?, ?)` uses index | Degrades — `OFFSET 10000` scans and discards 10K rows |
| Random page access | Not supported — must traverse sequentially | Supported — `offset = (page - 1) × size` |
| Infinite scroll / real-time feeds | Natural fit — no duplicates as data changes | Breaks — new items shift every subsequent page |
| Total count | Expensive — requires separate `COUNT(*)` query | Easy — `COUNT(*)` comes naturally with offset queries |
| Client complexity | Must store and forward opaque cursor string | Simple page number arithmetic |
| Relay Connection spec | Native — designed for this pattern | Can be adapted but feels forced |
| Bidirectional traversal | Built-in — `hasPreviousPage` + `before` cursor | Possible but needs extra state management |

sections.title: The Decision Isn't Always One or the Other
sections.content:
**Default to cursors** for any list that users scroll through — feeds, search results, notification lists, order histories. These are exactly the cases where data changes between page fetches, and where duplicates or missing items are most visible and annoying. The Relay Connection spec (`first`, `after`, `edges`, `pageInfo`) gives you a standardized contract that mobile and web clients can share.

The cursor itself should be **opaque** — base64-encode the sort key plus a tie-breaker (usually primary key) so clients can't construct cursors manually or depend on internal structure. Always include a unique tie-breaker in the sort: if many rows share the same `created_at` timestamp, `WHERE created_at > ?` alone produces non-deterministic results. Use `WHERE (created_at, id) > (?, ?)` to guarantee uniqueness.

On the database side, cursors translate to **keyset pagination** — a `WHERE` clause on the sort columns instead of `OFFSET`. This is dramatically faster on deep pages. `OFFSET 100000` forces the database to read and discard 100,000 rows before returning your actual results. A keyset `WHERE (created_at, id) > ('2025-01-10', 50000)` seeks directly to the right position in the index — near-constant cost regardless of depth.

**Use offset pagination only when** random page access is a genuine requirement — admin dashboards, support tooling, or internal grids where users need to jump to a specific page number. Accept the trade-offs: possible duplicates on actively changing data, degrading performance on deep pages, and the need for a `COUNT(*)` query that can be expensive on large tables.

For Spring Data JPA, avoid using `Pageable` with `OFFSET` for cursor-paginated lists. Instead, write explicit repository methods with `@Query` that translate cursors into `WHERE` clauses — `Pageable` always generates `OFFSET` SQL under the hood.

sections.title: Relay-Spec Connections — SDL + Spring for GraphQL Resolver
Spring for GraphQL — Keyset Pagination Behind the Connection
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Offset instability is invisible in testing** — inserts and deletes between page fetches shift the window, causing duplicates or skipped items.
- **Keyset queries stay constant-cost on deep pages** — `WHERE (created_at, id) > (?, ?)` index-seeks directly instead of scanning and discarding like.
- **Cursors must include a unique tie-breaker** — sorting by `created_at` alone produces non-deterministic results when rows share timestamps.
- **Relay Connections standardize the contract** — `first/after`, `edges/node`, `pageInfo` with `hasNextPage` give clients one pagination API to implement.
- **Spring Data `Pageable` always generates OFFSET** — for cursor pagination, write explicit `@Query` methods with keyset `WHERE` clauses instead of.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
GraphQL list pagination comes down to a choice between stability and simplicity. Offset pagination is simpler to implement but produces incorrect results under concurrent data changes. Cursor-based pagination is more reliable and performs better at depth.

**Why offset pagination fails in practice:**
- With offset pagination, if a row is inserted between page fetches, the window shifts — users see duplicates or skip items entirely; for infinite-scroll UIs with concurrent data changes, this is a poor user experience
- The instability is invisible in testing because it only manifests with real concurrent data changes; most test scenarios use static datasets

**Cursor-based pagination — how it works:**
- Cursors anchor to the last seen sort key plus a unique tie-breaker like the primary key, so the next page is always consistent regardless of what was inserted or deleted between fetches
- On the database side, it translates to a keyset query — `WHERE (created_at, id) > (?, ?)` — which index-seeks directly to the right position; `OFFSET 10000` forces the database to scan and discard ten thousand rows, growing slower as pages increase

**Relay Connection pattern:**
- The Relay Connection shape — `edges`, `node`, `cursor`, `pageInfo` with `hasNextPage` — is the standard that gives mobile and web clients one consistent pagination contract; it also provides room for edge-level metadata without breaking changes
- Cursors must include a unique tie-breaker — sorting by `created_at` alone produces non-deterministic results when rows share timestamps; compound `(created_at, id)` guarantees uniqueness

**Spring Data caveat:**
- `Pageable` in Spring Data always generates OFFSET SQL under the hood — for cursor pagination, write explicit `@Query` methods with keyset WHERE clauses

I recommend cursors for anything user-facing with concurrent data changes, and offset only for internal admin grids where page-jumping is a hard requirement and data consistency is lower priority.

questions.question: How does error handling work in GraphQL and how do you implement it in Spring Boot?
questions.title: GraphQL Error Handling in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: **GraphQL** always returns HTTP 200 with a JSON body. Errors appear in a top-level errors array alongside partial data. Spring for GraphQL provides DataFetcherExceptionResolver to map exceptions to GraphQLError objects. You should distinguish between user errors (validation failures, returned as data in the payload) and system errors (returned in the errors array).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand GraphQL's "HTTP 200 with top-level `errors`" shape, can classify errors (validation, authorization, unexpected) and return partial data, and use `DataFetcherExceptionResolver` in Spring for GraphQL.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Letting a raw Java stack trace leak into the `errors[0].message` field — exposes internals and confuses clients. Or conflating HTTP status errors (400/500) with GraphQL errors — a valid GraphQL response is always 200 unless the body itself was malformed.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss error classification (`ErrorType.BAD_REQUEST`, `UNAUTHORIZED`, `FORBIDDEN`, `NOT_FOUND`, `INTERNAL_ERROR`), carrying extension fields like `code` and `traceId`, partial responses with per-field nulls, and Apollo/Relay client error handling conventions.

sections.title: Why Your REST Instincts Are Wrong Here — HTTP 200 Is the Only Status Code
sections.content:
Developers coming from REST expect HTTP status codes to signal errors — 404 for not found, 403 for forbidden, 500 for server errors.
- GraphQL throws that mental model away.
- Every response returns **HTTP 200**, and the body always has two top-level fields: `data` (which may contain partial results) and `errors` (an array of error objects).
- Both can be present simultaneously.

This design exists because GraphQL supports **partial success**.
- A single query might fetch a user's profile, their orders, and their recommendations.
- If the recommendations resolver fails but the other two succeed, the response contains valid data for profile and orders, plus an error entry for recommendations.
- Returning HTTP 500 would discard the successful results.
- Returning HTTP 200 with an `errors` array preserves what worked while reporting what didn't.

The consequence for API development is fundamental: clients can never rely on HTTP status codes to detect errors.
- They must always inspect the `errors` array.
- And server-side, you need to classify errors — validation failures (the user did something wrong) versus system failures (something broke) — because the client handles these differently.
- A validation error maps to a form field; a system error triggers a retry or a generic error message.

In Spring for GraphQL, unhandled exceptions become `INTERNAL_ERROR` entries in the errors array with sanitized messages — no stack traces leak to clients. Custom exception mapping through `DataFetcherExceptionResolver` lets you control the error type, message, and metadata for each exception class.

sections.title: Map Domain Exceptions to Typed GraphQL Errors
Errors-as-Data on Mutation Payloads — The Pattern That Separates Good from Great APIs
Null Bubbling — The Error Propagation Behavior That Erases Responses
Key Points
sections.content:
- **HTTP 200 always, `errors` array for failures** — clients must parse the JSON body, not status codes.
- **`DataFetcherExceptionResolver` maps exceptions to typed errors** — domain exceptions become `NOT_FOUND` or `FORBIDDEN` with safe `extensions`.
- **`extensions.code` is the machine-readable contract** — clients branch on `code`, never on `message`.
- **`UserError` in mutation payloads separates validation from system failures** — field-level validation maps to form inputs.
- **Null bubbling erases entire responses from a single failure** — a non-null field failure cascades upward.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The biggest mental shift from REST to GraphQL error handling is that GraphQL always returns HTTP 200. Errors don't live in status codes — they live in a top-level `errors` array alongside whatever data succeeded. Partial success is normal: a response can return 49 books successfully and an error for the 50th, all in the same JSON body.

**How error mapping works in Spring:**
- Extend `DataFetcherExceptionResolverAdapter` to map Java exceptions to GraphQL errors; domain exceptions like `BookNotFoundException` become typed errors with a `NOT_FOUND` classification and safe metadata in the `extensions` map
- Clients branch on `extensions.code`, never on the human-readable message — messages are for humans, codes are for client logic; the `path` field identifies exactly which query field triggered the error
- Unhandled exceptions auto-sanitize to `INTERNAL_ERROR` so stack traces never leak to clients

**Validation errors — errors-as-data pattern:**
- For mutation validation, return a payload type with a `UserError` list that maps each error to a form field rather than throwing exceptions; clients map `field: "title"` to form inputs programmatically
- Reserve the top-level `errors` array for unexpected system failures — things the client can't recover from — and `UserError` for business validation failures

**Null bubbling — the production gotcha:**
- If a non-null field's resolver throws, GraphQL nulls the parent; if the parent is also non-null, it keeps cascading upward; a single author resolver failure can erase an entire list of 50 books if every ancestor is marked non-null
- Default fields to nullable unless they're truly invariant like `id`; tightening nullability later is non-breaking, loosening it is breaking

I recommend implementing `DataFetcherExceptionResolver` from day one and testing that specific exceptions produce specific `extensions.code` values — without explicit error mapping, every failure looks like `INTERNAL_ERROR` in client logs.

sections.title: Why REST Testing Patterns Don't Transfer Directly to GraphQL
sections.content:
In REST testing, you assert on HTTP status codes, response bodies, and headers — `MockMvc.perform(get("/api/books/1")).andExpect(status().isOk())`.
- With GraphQL, every request returns HTTP 200, the response body contains both `data` and `errors` arrays, and a single endpoint handles every operation.
- The testing tools that work for REST — status code assertions, path-based routing tests — don't capture the things that actually break in GraphQL: wrong field names in queries, missing schema mappings, resolver wiring bugs, and error classification.

Spring for GraphQL ships a dedicated testing module that addresses this gap.
- **`GraphQlTester`** provides a fluent API for executing query documents and asserting on JSON paths within the response.
- You write the query as a string, execute it against the engine (with or without HTTP), and assert on specific fields, error classifications, and nested data structures.

The testing strategy has two tiers.
- **Slice tests** with `@GraphQlTest` load only the GraphQL controller, the schema, and the exception resolvers — no database, no security filters.
- They run in milliseconds and catch most resolver wiring bugs.
- **Integration tests** with `@SpringBootTest` and `HttpGraphQlTester` exercise the full stack including JWT authentication, real repositories, DataLoader batching, and error handling.
- Together, these two tiers give you fast feedback during development and production confidence before deployment.

Testing Mutations and Error Scenarios — Where Most Teams Under-Invest
Integration Tests with HttpGraphQlTester — Full Stack Through HTTP
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@GraphQlTest` loads only the GraphQL slice** — controller, schema, and exception resolvers; services are `@MockBean`.
- **Path-based assertions prevent brittle tests** — `.path("books[0].title")` asserts on the contract that matters.
- **Error classification testing is non-optional** — verify that `BookNotFoundException` becomes `NOT_FOUND` and `AccessDeniedException` becomes.
- **`HttpGraphQlTester` exercises the full HTTP pipeline** — security filters, real repositories, DataLoader batching, and exception resolvers all.
- **Raw `WebTestClient` for transport edge cases** — content type, CORS, and malformed request handling are invisible to `GraphQlTester`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring for GraphQL ships `GraphQlTester`, which makes testing feel natural — you write a query document, execute it, and assert on JSON paths with a fluent API rather than brittle string equality on entire response bodies.

**Two-tier testing strategy:**
- For fast feedback, use `@GraphQlTest` slice tests with `@MockBean` services; these load only the controller, schema, and exception resolvers — no database, no security; they run in milliseconds and catch the most common bugs: method names that don't match schema fields, argument mismatches, and missing `@SchemaMapping` wiring
- For full stack coverage, use `@SpringBootTest` with `HttpGraphQlTester` on a random port; this exercises JWT authentication, real repositories, DataLoader batching, and error mapping

**Testing error scenarios — the critical gap:**
- The `.errors().satisfy()` API lets you verify that `BookNotFoundException` produces a `NOT_FOUND` classification with the right extensions, not just that "an error happened"
- Use `.mutate().header("Authorization", "Bearer " + jwt)` to simulate authenticated requests and verify that anonymous calls produce a `FORBIDDEN` error classification
- Without error path tests, every exception looks like `INTERNAL_ERROR` in client-facing responses and your monitoring

**Path-based assertions:**
- Use `.path("books[0].title")` assertions rather than comparing entire JSON responses; path-based assertions survive adding backward-compatible fields without breaking tests
- Assert on the specific fields that represent the contract, not the full response structure

**Transport-level tests:**
- Keep a few raw `WebTestClient` tests for CORS headers, content type, and malformed request handling — these are invisible to `GraphQlTester` but have caused real production issues

I recommend one test per resolver mapping, one test per error classification, and one test per authorization boundary as the minimum coverage floor for every GraphQL controller.

questions.question: How does gRPC compare to REST and GraphQL? When would you choose each?
questions.title: gRPC vs REST vs GraphQL
questions.direct_answer: **gRPC** wins for internal service-to-service: HTTP/2, **Protocol Buffers**, strong types, built-in deadlines and streaming — pick it when both sides are your own code. **REST** wins for public APIs: universal clients, CDN-cacheable reads, simple debugging with curl, great for CRUD over JSON. **GraphQL** wins for client-shaped reads: mobile and web UIs that need nested data in one round-trip, multiple clients with different data needs, schema-as-contract. Most real systems **blend** them — gRPC between services, REST for the public API, GraphQL as a BFF for rich UIs. Decide on workload shape (nested reads vs RPC writes vs streaming), audience (internal vs public), and caching needs (`Cache-Control` works for REST, not GraphQL).

sections.title: Three Protocols Solving Different Problems — Not Three Levels of Evolution
sections.content:
Most teams pick a communication protocol based on familiarity rather than fit.
- The result is predictable: REST everywhere creates cascading timeout chains when internal services need to exchange thousands of messages per second, while gRPC everywhere forces frontend teams to install protobuf compilers for a simple CRUD UI.
- Each of these three protocols was designed for a different audience and a different constraint.

**gRPC** was built by Google for internal service-to-service calls where performance and strict contracts matter.
- It uses HTTP/2 for multiplexed connections and Protocol Buffers for binary serialization — the combination produces payloads 5–10× smaller than JSON and eliminates per-request TCP setup overhead.
- **REST** was designed around resources and HTTP verbs for the widest possible client compatibility — browsers, curl, mobile apps, third-party partners all speak HTTP/JSON natively.
- **GraphQL** was created at Facebook to solve a mobile-specific problem: screens that need data from five different backend resources shouldn't require five round trips or receive fields they don't display.

The trap is treating this as a ranking.
- Teams that deploy gRPC for everything lose REST's debuggability at the edge — you can't ask a partner to install protobuf tooling to test an integration.
- Teams that use REST internally burn CPU on JSON parsing at high throughput when protobuf would be 10× more efficient.
- The strongest architectures combine all three — gRPC on internal hot paths, REST for external consumers, GraphQL for complex frontend aggregation — matching protocol to consumer need rather than team preference.

sections.title: What Each Protocol Optimizes For — And What It Sacrifices
sections.content:
| Dimension | gRPC | REST | GraphQL |
|---|---|---|---|
| Transport | HTTP/2 (multiplexed, header-compressed) | HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 | HTTP (typically 1.1) |
| Data format | Binary Protobuf (3–10× smaller) | JSON text (human-readable) | JSON text (human-readable) |
| Type safety | Mandatory `.proto` contracts | Optional (OpenAPI/Swagger) | Mandatory schema |
| Streaming | Bidirectional streaming built-in | SSE or WebSocket workarounds | Subscriptions only |
| Browser support | Requires grpc-web proxy | Native — works everywhere | Native — works everywhere |
| Over-fetching | Contract-controlled fields | Common — fixed response shapes | Client specifies exact fields |
| Debugging | Requires grpcurl or Bloom RPC | Trivial — curl, Postman, browser | Moderate — GraphiQL, Apollo |
| Code generation | Auto-generated stubs (mandatory) | Optional (OpenAPI codegen) | Schema-driven codegen |
| Performance | Very high at scale | Moderate | Moderate (N+1 query risk) |
| Best fit | Internal microservices, high-RPS paths | Public APIs, external consumers | Complex frontend aggregation |

sections.title: The Decision Framework: Match Protocol to Consumer, Not to Preference
sections.content:
**Choose gRPC when** the caller is an internal service you control, call frequency is high (thousands per second), and payload efficiency matters. Protobuf's compiled schema catches breaking changes at build time — a renamed field that would silently break REST clients at runtime produces a compile error with gRPC. At Uber, the internal mesh handles millions of gRPC calls per second; the latency savings compound when a single user request traverses 5+ service hops.

**Choose REST when** external consumers call your API — browsers, mobile apps, third-party partners. Every developer on earth can test a REST endpoint with curl. CDN caching works natively with HTTP semantics. OAuth flows, webhooks, and API management platforms all assume REST. Forcing external consumers to install protobuf tooling creates friction that eliminates any performance advantage.

**Choose GraphQL when** frontend teams build complex UIs that aggregate data from multiple backend domains and screen-to-screen data requirements vary widely. The risk is that GraphQL shifts query complexity to the server — without depth limiting and query cost analysis, one deeply nested query can fan out into hundreds of database calls. Use persisted queries in production to cap complexity.

Most mature architectures use at least two of these: gRPC inside the service mesh for throughput, REST or a BFF GraphQL gateway at the edge. The anti-pattern is picking one and forcing every interaction through it.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
gRPC, REST, and GraphQL are not competing technologies — they solve different coupling problems, and the right choice depends on who is calling, at what frequency, and whether the caller is internal or external.

**gRPC — internal high-RPS paths:**
- My default for internal service-to-service calls where performance matters: Protobuf payloads are 5–10× smaller than JSON, and HTTP/2 multiplexing means multiple RPCs share one TCP connection, eliminating the per-request TLS handshake cost
- Strict schema contracts via `.proto` files catch breaking changes at compile time — a renamed field that would silently break REST consumers at runtime produces a build error with generated stubs
- The constraint: gRPC requires a grpc-web proxy for browser clients; HTTP/2 trailers are not accessible from browser JavaScript, so anything external-facing needs REST at the edge

**REST — external-facing, universal:**
- My default for anything external-facing: every developer knows how to call a REST API with curl, CDN caching works natively, and API management tooling assumes HTTP/JSON
- Requiring external partners to install protobuf compilers eliminates any performance advantage; REST's universality is the advantage
- For internal calls at moderate frequencies, REST is still fine because debugging simplicity outweighs microsecond differences

**GraphQL — complex frontend aggregation:**
- Fills the niche where frontend screens need data from multiple backend domains with varying field requirements
- The catch: without depth limiting and query cost analysis, one deeply nested query can generate hundreds of database calls; use persisted queries in production to control the query surface

**The architectural combination:**
- The strongest production architectures combine all three: gRPC inside the mesh for throughput, REST at the edge for universal compatibility, GraphQL for complex frontend aggregation behind a BFF layer

I recommend gRPC when the caller is a service you control and call frequency is high, REST for external callers, and GraphQL when frontends need flexible data shapes from multiple domains.
